## How Should Modern Technical Slides Be Structured?

<span class="kicker">Guiding Principle</span>

Every slide must answer **one specific question** with absolute visual clarity.

::: {.key-idea}
::: {.key-idea-title}
💡 Fundamental Design Law [@vaswani2017attention]
:::
**High-impact default:** One primary question, one intuitive visual or equation anchor, and zero clutter. Explanations, edge cases, and derivations belong in speaker notes.
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
<div class="card-title">🎯 Cognitive Load Management</div>
Dense text slides force the audience to choose between reading paragraphs and listening to the lecturer. Clean slides allow the instructor to lead the narrative.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .card-glow}
<div class="card-title">⚡ Visual Anchor Dominance</div>
A strong central figure or formatted equation card anchors the concept in memory 3× more effectively than bulleted text.
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Emphasize the cognitive science behind minimal, focused slide decks for graduate-level courses.
When designing a slide:
1. Define the single question the slide answers.
2. Provide a bold visual or mathematical answer.
3. Put the nuance in speaker notes to guide your lecture narration.
:::

## Why Factorize Spatial and Channel Convolutions?

<span class="kicker">Computational Factorization</span>

::: {.columns .valign-center}

::: {.column width="52%"}

<div class="column-title">Separating Space from Channels</div>

Standard convolution couples spatial filtering with channel mixing. **Depthwise separable convolutions** [@howard2017mobilenets] factorize this into two distinct steps:

1. **Depthwise:** Spatial filtering per channel ($K \times K \times 1$)
2. **Pointwise:** Linear combination across channels ($1 \times 1 \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}$)

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-term}
📐 Computational Factorization
:::
Decomposing multidimensional tensor operations into orthogonal rank-1 operators drastically cuts FLOPs with negligible accuracy loss.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="48%"}

$$
\mathrm{FLOPs}_{\text{standard}} = H \cdot W \cdot C_{\text{in}} \cdot C_{\text{out}} \cdot K^2
$$

$$
\mathrm{FLOPs}_{\text{separable}} = H \cdot W \cdot C_{\text{in}} \cdot K^2 + H \cdot W \cdot C_{\text{in}} \cdot C_{\text{out}}
$$

::: {.card .card-muted}
$$\text{Efficiency Gain} \approx \frac{1}{N} + \frac{1}{K^2} \approx \mathbf{8\text{–}9\times \text{ Reduction}}$$
:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Walking through the math:
- In a standard $3 \times 3$ convolution, $K=3 \implies K^2 = 9$.
- Factorization separates spatial filtering from cross-channel linear combination.
- As $C_{\text{out}}$ grows large, $\frac{1}{C_{\text{out}}} \to 0$, leaving an asymptotic computational saving of $\approx 9\times$.
- This principle laid the foundation for MobileNet, Xception, and modern efficient vision backbones.
:::

## How Is Scaled Dot-Product Attention Formulated?

<span class="kicker">Mathematical Formulation</span>

::: {.formula-card}
::: {.formula-header}
Core Attention Mechanism [@vaswani2017attention]
:::

$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
$$

::: {.formula-legend}
Where $Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}$ and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_v}$ denote query, key, and value matrices, and $\sqrt{d_k}$ is the temperature scaling factor.
:::
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.info-box}
::: {.info-box-title}
ℹ️ Scaling Rationale
:::
Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ prevents the dot products from growing excessively large in high dimensions, which would push the softmax function into regions with vanishingly small gradients.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.warning}
::: {.warning-title}
⚠️ Memory IO Bottleneck
:::
Computing $Q K^T$ materializes an $N \times N$ attention matrix in HBM, creating an $O(N^2)$ memory IO bottleneck resolved by tiling algorithms like FlashAttention [@dao2022flashattention].
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Speaker points for attention formulation:
- Explain why standard dot products without scaling cause softmax saturation when $d_k \ge 64$.
- Highlight that $Q K^T$ produces an $N \times N$ matrix whose materialization in high-bandwidth memory is the primary memory bottleneck.
- Mention how FlashAttention solves this via SRAM tiling and online softmax rescaling.
:::

## What Are the Primary Multimodal Fusion Paradigms?

<span class="kicker">Taxonomy Overview</span>

::: {.grid-3}

::: {.card}
[Early Fusion]{.badge .badge-image}

<div class="card-title">Direct Concatenation</div>

Raw or patch-level tokens are concatenated into a single sequence before the transformer backbone.

- **Pros:** Full bidirectional cross-modal attention at every layer.
- **Cons:** Quadratic compute scaling over long sequences.
:::

::: {.card .card-accent}
[Cross-Attention]{.badge .badge-video}

<div class="card-title">Latent Cross-Fusion</div>

Modalities are processed in dedicated backbones and cross-attended in intermediary layers.

- **Pros:** Modular pretraining and decoupled representations.
- **Cons:** Asymmetric flow and potential alignment bottlenecks.
:::

::: {.card}
[Native Omni]{.badge .badge-unified}

<div class="card-title">Unified Token Stream</div>

Universal token vocabulary interleaves text, vision patches, and audio frames in a single autoregressive stream.

- **Pros:** True omni-modal zero-shot reasoning.
- **Cons:** Complex multi-task loss balancing and high VRAM.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Compare the three evolutionary stages of multimodal architecture:
1. Early fusion works well for small inputs but explodes in compute for video/audio.
2. Cross-attention (Flamingo, LLaVA, BLIP) is standard for modular deployment.
3. Native omni-modal models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Mini-Omni) process everything in a single joint token stream for native cross-modality understanding.
:::

## What Are the Real-World Gains of FP8 Quantization?

<span class="kicker">Performance Benchmarks</span>

::: {.metric-row}

::: {.metric-card}
<div class="metric-value">4.2×</div>
<div class="metric-label">Inference Speedup</div>
<span class="metric-delta positive">+320% Token/s</span>
:::

::: {.metric-card}
<div class="metric-value">75%</div>
<div class="metric-label">VRAM Reduction</div>
<span class="metric-delta positive">4-bit AWQ Quant</span>
:::

::: {.metric-card}
<div class="metric-value">−0.2%</div>
<div class="metric-label">MMLU Accuracy Delta</div>
<span class="metric-delta negative">Negligible Loss</span>
:::

::: {.metric-card}
<div class="metric-value">128k</div>
<div class="metric-label">Context Window</div>
<span class="metric-delta positive">FlashAttention-3</span>
:::

:::

::: {.warning}
::: {.warning-title}
⚠️ Memory Bandwidth Constraint
:::
Theoretical FLOP reductions only translate to wall-clock latency gains when the kernel is compute-bound. In autoregressive token generation with small batch sizes, latency is strictly bound by High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) bandwidth.
:::

::: {.notes}
Guide to interpreting metric counters:
- Walk through the Roofline Model: Arithmetic Intensity $I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred}}$.
- Quantization reduces memory transfer volume per token, moving memory-bound kernels closer to compute saturation.
- Show students how 4-bit weight compression allows a 70B parameter model to fit onto a single 48GB GPU (e.g. RTX 6000 Ada or 2x RTX 4090).
:::

## Dense vs Sparse: How Do MoE Models Compare?

<span class="kicker">Architectural Trade-Offs</span>

::: {.compare-container}

::: {.compare-card .compare-con}
::: {.compare-header}
<span>Dense Transformer Baseline</span>
[Standard]{.badge .badge-video}
:::

- Every parameter is active for every input token
- Fixed computational cost proportional to total parameter count $P_{\text{total}}$
- Compute-bound at large batch sizes, but excessive FLOP waste on simple tokens
- Higher energy footprint per output token

$$C_{\text{dense}} = 2 \cdot N \cdot P_{\text{total}}$$

:::

::: {.compare-card .compare-pro}
::: {.compare-header}
<span>Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE)</span>
[Efficient]{.badge .badge-unified}
:::

- Top-$k$ gating dynamically routes tokens to specialized feedforward experts
- Constant computational budget with massive capacity: $P_{\text{active}} \ll P_{\text{total}}$
- Higher throughput per watt and superior scaling laws
- Expert parallelism requires high inter-GPU interconnect bandwidth

$$C_{\text{MoE}} = 2 \cdot N \cdot P_{\text{active}}$$

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Comparison analysis:
- Point out why frontier labs transitioned from dense scaling to MoE architectures.
- Discuss the tradeoff: MoE decouples parameter capacity from FLOP compute per token, but increases total memory footprint and communication overhead across GPU clusters.
:::

## What Is the End-to-End Multimodal Execution Flow?

<span class="kicker">Execution Pipeline</span>

::: {.step-flow}

::: {.step-flow-item}
<div class="step-number">Step 01</div>
<div class="step-title">Tokenization</div>
<div class="step-desc">Discretize audio waveforms, visual image patches, and text into unified discrete token IDs.</div>
:::

::: {.step-flow-item}
<div class="step-number">Step 02</div>
<div class="step-title">Alignment</div>
<div class="step-desc">Project modality latents into a shared dimensional embedding space via projection layers.</div>
:::

::: {.step-flow-item}
<div class="step-number">Step 03</div>
<div class="step-title">Transformer Core</div>
<div class="step-desc">Deep autoregressive processing with rotary embeddings, self-attention, and MoE routing.</div>
:::

::: {.step-flow-item}
<div class="step-number">Step 04</div>
<div class="step-title">Detokenization</div>
<div class="step-desc">Decode generated output tokens into waveforms, synthesized frames, or robotic actions.</div>
:::

:::

::: {.info-box}
::: {.info-box-title}
ℹ️ Continuous vs Discrete Tokenization
:::
While text is inherently discrete, continuous modalities (audio waveforms and image pixels) require neural audio codecs (e.g., DAC, EnCodec) or continuous diffusion decoders to reconstruct high-fidelity outputs.
:::

::: {.notes}
Process flow walk-through:
- Step 1 converts disparate physical signals into sequences of integer tokens or continuous feature vectors.
- Step 2 ensures dimensional compatibility and semantic alignment across modalities.
- Step 3 applies universal sequence modeling across time and modalities.
- Step 4 routes tokens to modality-specific decoders (e.g. HiFi-GAN for audio, VAE for images).
:::

## How Is RMSNorm Implemented in PyTorch?

<span class="kicker">Implementation Reference</span>

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    """Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019)."""
    def __init__(self, dim: int, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim))

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Compute root mean square across last dimension without mean centering
        rms = torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return x * rms * self.weight
```

::: {.card .card-muted .card-compact}
<span class="small">**System Optimization Insight:** RMSNorm eliminates the mean subtraction pass required by standard LayerNorm ($O(2N)$ down to $O(N)$ reads), saving ~7% HBM bandwidth per transformer layer.</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Code explanation:
- Review the difference between LayerNorm and RMSNorm: LayerNorm computes both mean and variance $\mu, \sigma^2$, requiring two reduction passes over memory.
- RMSNorm enforces scale invariance by computing only the root mean square $\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum x_i^2}$.
- Note the use of `torch.rsqrt` for optimized reciprocal square root instruction execution on CUDA Tensor Cores.
:::

## Checkpoint: What Dictates Real-World LLM Generation Speed?

::: {.checkpoint-box}

::: {.checkpoint-header}
❓ Checkpoint 01 • Memory vs Compute Bottlenecks
:::

::: {.checkpoint-question}
What is the primary hardware bottleneck during autoregressive token generation at batch size 1 on modern GPUs?
:::

::: {.checkpoint-options}

::: {.checkpoint-option}
A. Tensor Core peak FLOP/s compute throughput (Compute Bound)
:::

::: {.checkpoint-option .correct}
B. High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) Transfer Rate (Memory Bandwidth Bound)
:::

::: {.checkpoint-option}
C. CPU-to-GPU PCIe host-device interconnect latency
:::

::: {.checkpoint-option}
D. KV-cache allocation fragmentation in PyTorch allocator
:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
**Correct Answer: B.**
In autoregressive generation at batch size 1, every forward pass reads the entire model parameter tensor ($2P$ bytes in FP16) from HBM into on-chip SRAM to generate just 1 token ($2P$ FLOPs).
Arithmetic intensity:
$$I = \frac{2P\text{ FLOPs}}{2P\text{ Bytes}} = 1\text{ FLOP/Byte}$$
On an NVIDIA A100 (Peak compute 312 TFLOP/s, HBM bandwidth 2039 GB/s), the ridge point is $I_{\text{ridge}} \approx 153\text{ FLOP/Byte}$. Since $1 \ll 153$, batch size 1 generation is severely memory-bandwidth bound.
:::

## What Is the Core Takeaway for System Optimization?

<span class="kicker">Synthesis & Key Takeaway</span>

::: {.takeaway}
<div class="takeaway-title">Final Synthesis</div>
<div class="takeaway-message">
FLOPs measure theoretical compute, but memory bandwidth dictates real-world latency. Always profile memory traffic before optimizing math operations.
</div>
:::

::: {.notes}
Final synthesis for the audience:
- Reiterate that algorithms that look computationally heavy on paper may run faster than sparse algorithms if they are IO-efficient.
- Encourage students to make roofline analysis and memory bandwidth profiling standard practice.
:::
